To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the complexity of the glioblastoma tumor microenvironment, including the presence of multiple cell types, is an important factor in the failure of molecularly targeted therapies; (2) glioblastomas can be classified into four molecular subtypes that are associated with specific genetic abnormalities and clinical outcomes; and (3) the molecular classification of glioblastoma may help to identify patients who are most likely to benefit from molecularly targeted therapies.

(i) the complexity and adaptive nature of cancer impose challenges for targeted cancer therapy; (ii) the complexity of glioblastoma is reflected in its genomic landscape, which includes multiple mutations in signaling pathways, and in its molecular and phenotypic heterogeneity; (iii) the genomic landscape of glioblastomas is characterized by a high degree of heterogeneity and complexity, including a wide variety of genetic alterations in signaling pathways, including the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK
(1) glioblastoma is genomically complex and heterogeneous, and (2) new molecular diagnostics and targeted therapies are needed to improve outcomes for patients with glioblastoma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of molecular markers of glioblastoma that can be used for the development of new diagnostic and prognostic tests.
the development of new strategies in the molecular targeting of glioblastoma.
the development and implementation of novel strategies in targeted therapy of glioblastoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the new targeted agents is still experimental and that the best approach for the treatment of patients with glioblastoma is the standard treatment of temozolomide and radiotherapy.
the use of targeted therapy for the treatment of glioblastomas is still in the early stages.
the molecular targeting of cancer, as a strategy to improve cancer therapy, remains a challenge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
glioblastoma is an example of a molecularly complex cancer that is not driven by single mutations but is instead a pathway-driven disease that has evolved to adapt to the environment.
we have identified and characterized a novel pathway that is critical to the survival and proliferation of glioblastoma and that is a potential target for the development of new therapeutics.
gliomas are a model of a molecularly complex disease for which new genomic insight is being translated into new molecular diagnostic and treatment paradigms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have to be more sophisticated in our approach to cancer therapy.
we need to think about cancer as a moving target.

the complexity of glioblastoma and other cancers will require us to integrate genomic and functional biology to guide the development of new diagnostic strategies that are more likely to identify patients with glioblastoma who are likely to benefit from targeted therapy.
